name: Wei Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing nursing, and the week is mostly lectures on anatomy and a skills lab where we practise taking blood pressure on each other. I share a flat with three people near the tram line, and on Saturdays and Sundays I work in the kitchen of a care home, mostly peeling and washing up. My parents run a small dry cleaner and they cover my rent, but I pay for food and travel myself. I'm tired by Thursday, but I like it more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, that's what I expected anyway. Every few years someone says a machine will take over, and then the hospital still needs a person to turn a patient. I'd tell my flatmates not to panic over chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I don't trust the companies pushing it, so hype fits what I think. For me it means nothing changes, which is fine, but nothing changes about the money either. The loan is still there, and my parents' shop is quiet some months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd keep the weekend care home shifts, about 14 hours, and put £40 a week aside for the second-year placement costs. I'd also join the student nursing society, because it fights for better placement pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels steady, a bit boring even. A little worried because my parents' dry cleaner is already slow, and if it closes I can't ask them for rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which cost on your list worries you most while you study, and what would you do if money got tighter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is the one. My parents pay about 400 a month, and if the shop has a bad winter that's the first thing that stops. Then I'd go from 14 hours at the care home to 24 and probably fail an exam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Think about the day you finish your degree. What do you picture yourself doing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I picture a ward at six in the morning, doing handovers with a mug of tea, and a loan of about 40 thousand. Nurses are needed, so I think a job will exist. I just hope the hospital pays enough to live somewhere that isn't a shared flat.

say: I'd tell friends that **hype** always fades and hospitals will still need people.
I'd push the nursing society to keep fighting for **placement pay**.
think: Privately I worry less about AI than about **rent** if my parents' shop struggles.
I don't trust tech companies, so I expect little to really change.
do: Keep the care home **shifts** at about 14 hours a week.
Save **£40 a week** for placement costs next year.
Join the nursing society and its **placement pay** campaign.
feel: **Steady** but a bit stuck, because my family's money is the weak spot.
S0.quote: Every few years someone says a machine will take over, and then the hospital still needs a person to turn a patient.
fieldNote: Wei dismisses the **hype** quickly and moves straight to the money.
Distrust of big companies drives his views more than any knowledge of the tools.
The parents' dry cleaner is the real **fragility**, not his course.

steps.text: Keep working weekend shifts in the care home kitchen
Put £40 a week into a placement fund
Join the nursing society placement pay campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will hit offices before wards. I'd tell my flatmates who do business that they're the ones in the firing line. And I'd say the government should make employers pay for any retraining, not leave it to workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part of my course is thinking work, like care plans and charting, and I'd bet software takes the paperwork. I'd rather keep my hands on patients. I think wards will want fewer admin staff, so more of the job becomes real care, which suits me. But I don't trust the hospital to keep staffing levels up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and ask my tutor which parts of charting are being moved to software so I'm not caught out. I'd still not use any AI tool myself; I don't like how they take people's words. I'd talk to the union rep when I start my placement in second year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. It's the pace that gets me, because people say 'adjust' like it's easy and it isn't. I'm slow to pick up new things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which jobs in your field, or the part-time work you do now, would AI touch first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The care home kitchen would go first, I think. They already have an ordering system that suggests quantities, and the manager says one day it will place the orders itself. That's three of us sharing about 30 hours of shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change what you study, or how you study it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the degree the same, since the hands-on parts are the point. But I'd start paying more attention in the digital records class, even though I find it dull. If I'm going to be the one who stays at the bedside, I'd rather not be the one who can't use the screen.

say: I'd tell flatmates that **offices** will feel it before wards do.
I'd say **employers** should pay for retraining, not workers.
think: Charting will move to software, which leaves more **real care** for me.
I don't trust hospitals to keep **staffing** up when software saves time.
do: Ask my tutor which **paperwork** tasks are moving to software.
Pay more attention in the **digital records** class, even though it's dull.
Talk to the union rep when **placement** starts.
feel: **Uneasy** about the pace, since I'm slow with new technology.
S1.quote: If I'm going to be the one who stays at the bedside, I'd rather not be the one who can't use the screen.
fieldNote: Wei links change to **fairness**: who pays, who gets protected.
He stays opposed to AI tools but is quietly **hedging** in the records class.
His care home kitchen shifts are the first real exposure.

steps.text: Ask the tutor what charting moves to software
Talk to the placement union rep in second year
Keep the care home shifts while they last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's far too fast and nobody voted for it. I'd go to a rally if one existed, and I'd sign anything demanding the government slows it down or taxes the companies. Two years is nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared. If thinking work is gone by 2028, then hospital managers, accountants and my parents' customers are all affected, and my parents' shop depends on office workers bringing in shirts. I'd probably still have a job on the ward until the robots catch up around 2031, but I'd be paying a loan in a bad economy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents the same week and ask them honestly how much the shop can carry. I'd move to cheaper housing, maybe a room at my aunt's, and add care home hours. I'd also email my MP and join any group fighting for a basic income, because that's the real answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd feel sick for a few weeks. It feels like the ground moves and my family can't catch me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your family, and what would you do about your degree place and your loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my phone contract and stop buying anything for fun. I'd cook all meals, and I'd tell my parents to stop paying for my room so they keep money for the shop. If my parents lose the dry cleaner, who pays for a nurse's first year?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, who or what would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lean on my parents, my aunt and the union. I'd lean on my tutors too, because they'll know what the hospital plans. I wouldn't lean on companies or the government to have a plan, because they don't seem to have one.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** and nobody voted for it.
I'd sign anything that demands **taxes** on AI companies or a slower rollout.
think: My parents' **dry cleaner** depends on office workers, so their income is at risk.
I'd still have ward work until robots catch up, but a **loan** in a bad economy scares me.
do: Ask my parents honestly how much the **shop** can carry.
Move into a cheaper room at my **aunt's** place.
Email my **MP** and join a basic income campaign.
feel: **Heavy**, like the ground moves and my family can't catch me.
S2.quote: If my parents lose the dry cleaner, who pays for a nurse's first year?
fieldNote: Wei's fear is about **his parents' shop**, not his own job prospects.
His outlook turns him towards **collective action** and policy rather than personal reskilling.
He names no tools he would try, which fits his resistance.

steps.text: Ask parents how much the shop can carry
Move into a cheaper room at my aunt's
Add care home hours and cook all meals
Email the MP and join a basic income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's still time to push for rules. Five years is enough for unions to win a deal about who gets protected and who pays. I'd tell friends to get involved now, not after it's here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think I'd graduate right into it, and the hospital job would be fine at first because of hands-on work, but by the time I'm 24 thinking AI is everywhere. I'd be a nurse in a changing system with colleagues losing admin roles around me. That's anxious, but I'd have three years on the ward before the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take every placement hour I can, because experience is the thing that keeps nurses valuable. I'd put aside about £60 a month once I graduate. I'd get involved with the union branch early, and I'd learn the hospital's records system properly, though I'd still avoid chatbots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but a bit more in control than with two years. A date makes it easier to plan, though I'd still lie awake some nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in those five years compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The difference from two years is that I'd finish my degree before the worst of it. In the short version I'd be dropping out of everything to help my family. Here I'd stay and pay my own way a bit longer, and my parents could sell the shop slowly instead of in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At what point would you decide to stay on your course or change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd decide at the end of second year. If hospitals are cutting nursing places or the pay offer stays bad, I'd consider switching to something with more demand, maybe physiotherapy. But I'd stay if the wards are still short of staff, because short-staffed wards need hands.

say: I'd say five years is enough for **unions** to win real protections.
I'd tell friends to get involved **now**, not after it arrives.
think: I'd graduate right into it, and the **ward job** would hold until robots arrive.
Colleagues in **admin** roles would lose jobs around me, which would weigh on me.
do: Take every **placement** hour I can to build experience.
Put aside **£60 a month** once I graduate.
Join the **union** branch early and learn the hospital records system.
feel: **Anxious**, but more in control, because a date makes planning possible.
S3.quote: I'd stay if the wards are still short of staff, because short-staffed wards need hands.
fieldNote: A longer runway moves Wei from **panic** to planning, and he says so.
He sets a decision point at the **end of second year**.
He still treats the union and policy as the main defence.

steps.text: Take every extra placement hour on offer
Join the union branch in first year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and I'd tell people not to waste it. Governments should use it to build proper support, like retraining and income help. I'd say it again and again if I had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fairly settled. By 2036 I'd be 29, a few years into nursing, and the robots would arrive around 2039. I'd probably have ten good working years first. I'd worry about my parents, who would be near retirement and dependent on the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work on a ward, and try to buy a small flat by 30 if prices allow. I'd save for my parents' retirement, because the shop won't last that long. I'd get involved in the union early, and eventually I'd probably have to learn the new tools, though I'd resist for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A decade feels like something I can plan around, though one part of me thinks it's too far to be real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having ten years let you do that two years wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I could finish, build a career and put money aside for my parents. With two years I'd be firefighting. Time lets me be the person who helps my family instead of the person who needs help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a friend who's thinking of starting your degree next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a friend nursing is a good bet, because people will still need care and the hands-on part lasts longest. But I'd say join a union and don't ignore the technology the way I do. Whatever time you get, use it to be useful in ways a machine isn't.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and governments shouldn't waste it.
I'd push for proper **retraining** and income support.
think: I'd have about **ten working years** on a ward before robots arrive.
My real worry is my **parents'** retirement, since the shop won't last.
do: Finish the degree and work on a **ward**.
Save for my parents' **retirement** alongside my own flat deposit.
Join the **union** early and learn the new tools eventually.
feel: **Calm enough**, though ten years feels too far away to be real.
S4.quote: Time lets me be the person who helps my family instead of the person who needs help.
fieldNote: Wei's mood softens with time, but **family money** still holds it at uneasy.
He plans for his **parents' retirement** before his own flat.
Even here he admits he will have to learn the tools in the end.

steps.text: Work on a ward after graduating
Save for parents' retirement and a flat deposit
Learn the ward's new tools once colleagues do

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because everything lands before my family or the hospital can prepare. What would help is a real safety net: retraining paid for by employers, rent support for students, and small shops like my parents' being protected somehow.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't against technology, we just don't trust who's in charge of it. I'd like to be asked before things happen to us, not after.

headlineQuote: I'd like to be asked before things happen to us, not after.
portrait: Wei is a **nursing** first-year, 19, in a shared flat, helped by his parents' dry cleaner income.
He works weekends in a **care home** kitchen and has never used an AI tool.
He is progressive, distrusts **big companies**, and leans on unions and policy for protection.
His fear is about his **parents' shop** more than his own job.
He moves from uneasy to anxious as the warning time shrinks to two or five years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, because family and hospitals couldn't prepare.
whatWouldHelp: Employer-paid **retraining**, rent support for students and protection for small family shops.
